items.prompt: Is delegation best thought of as a binary choice (do it myself vs. hand it off entirely)?
choices: Yes — either you delegate a task or you don't
No — it's a spectrum of how much autonomy the delegate has, from 'do exactly this' to 'full autonomy, no need to report'
Yes, but only for technical tasks
No — delegation only applies to entire projects, never individual decisions
items.explanation: Delegation exists on a spectrum of autonomy levels, not as a single on/off switch — treating it as binary is exactly what leaves the actual level unspecified and open to mismatched assumptions.
items.reference:

...

6. Full autonomy, no need to report

Why: most delegation failures come from a gap between two points on this spectrum, not from delegating at all vs. not.
items.learnMore:
A spectrum, not a switch

Thinking of delegation as binary hides the real decision that has to be made every time: not whether to delegate, but how much autonomy to hand over for this specific task.

Common mistake

Treating 'I delegated it' as a complete instruction, when the actual autonomy level was never specified.

items.prompt: What's the single most important habit this unit recommends for effective delegation?
choices: Always delegate the maximum possible autonomy to show trust
Name the autonomy level out loud, every time — don't assume it's obvious from context or that it carries over from last time
Only delegate tasks you could do yourself
Write a formal delegation document for every task
items.explanation: Making the level explicit — rather than assuming it's understood — is the core fix this unit teaches, directly addressing the exact gap that caused the CI-vendor incident.
items.reference:
Not a level: "take care of it"

A level: "research options and bring me a recommendation before we commit"

Why: vague delegation verbs get filled in by whichever assumption feels natural to each person.
items.learnMore:
Saying it out loud

The fix in this unit isn't a complicated process — it's a habit of specificity. Naming the level costs one extra sentence and prevents the exact kind of mismatch the incident describes.

Common mistake

Assuming that because a level felt obvious to you, it was equally obvious to the person receiving the delegation.

items.prompt: Is handing someone the highest possible autonomy level always the best form of delegation?
choices: Yes — maximum autonomy always shows the most trust and empowerment
No — high autonomy on a decision the delegate lacks context for isn't empowering, it's setting them up to make an avoidable mistake
Yes, as long as the delegate is generally competent
No — the highest level should never be used under any circumstances
items.explanation: The right level depends on stakes and context, not a blanket preference for maximum autonomy — handing over full authority on something the delegate doesn't yet have context for is exactly what produced the CI-vendor incident.
items.reference:
Full autonomy on a decision with no relevant context = an avoidable mistake waiting to happen, not empowerment.

Why: the level should track stakes and context, not a fixed philosophy of 'always delegate maximally.'
items.learnMore:
Empowerment vs. setting someone up to fail

A well-meaning manager can genuinely believe they're empowering someone by handing over full autonomy, while actually removing the one safety check (a review before commitment) that would have caught an avoidable mistake.

Common mistake

Equating 'high autonomy' with 'good management' as a blanket rule, regardless of the specific task's stakes.

The risk only applies to junior employees, never experienced ones

items.explanation: A blanket high-autonomy policy ignores the two factors that should actually drive the level choice — stakes and context — which is exactly how the CI-vendor incident happened even though the report was doing careful, well-intentioned work.

items.prompt: "Trust but verify" is sometimes dismissed as a contradiction. How does this unit resolve that?
choices: It doesn't resolve it — trust and verification really are incompatible
It's a real middle ground: a specific, light-touch check-in point (not reviewing every step) that protects against a costly mismatch without requiring constant oversight
It means trusting the delegate completely and never verifying anything
It means verifying every single decision the delegate makes, with trust as an afterthought
items.explanation: A single, well-placed check-in point — like 'loop me in before signing anything' — is genuinely compatible with high trust; it's not the same as reviewing every step, which would be micromanagement.
items.reference:
"Loop me in once you've narrowed it to two or three finalists, before signing."

Why: a single, specific trigger point protects against a costly mismatch without requiring step-by-step oversight.
items.learnMore:
A named trigger, not constant checking

The value of 'trust but verify' comes entirely from HOW the verify part is scoped. A vague promise to 'check in sometimes' provides little protection; a specific trigger tied to the moment that actually matters (before an irreversible commitment) provides real protection with minimal overhead.

Common mistake

Treating 'trust but verify' as license to check in constantly 'just in case,' which defeats the purpose of delegating at all.

items.prompt: Where did the manager and report actually sit on the six-level spectrum in the CI-vendor incident?

items.explanation: The manager was operating at Level 3 (wanting a recommendation before deciding); the report was operating at Level 5 (deciding and informing afterward) — a two-level gap that, on a low-stakes task, might never have mattered.
items.reference:
Manager: Level 3 — recommend, I approve

Report: Level 5 — decide and act, tell me after

Why: a two-level gap on a high-stakes, hard-to-reverse decision is what turned an unstated assumption into a real incident.
items.learnMore:

Common mistake

items.prompt: What are the two questions L2 recommends asking to choose a delegation level?
choices: How senior is the delegate, and how busy is the manager?
How reversible/expensive is a wrong decision, and how much relevant context does the delegate already have for THIS specific decision?
How much does the manager like the delegate, and how urgent is the deadline?
How many people are on the team, and what's the company's org chart?
items.explanation: These two factors — reversibility/cost of a wrong call, and the delegate's existing context for this specific decision — are what should drive the level choice, not general seniority or unrelated factors.
items.reference:
1. How reversible/expensive is a wrong call?

2. How much relevant context does the delegate have for THIS decision?

Why: a one-year vendor contract with a first-time evaluator points toward a lower autonomy level on both counts.
items.learnMore:
Two factors, asked together

Neither question alone is sufficient — a highly reversible decision might warrant high autonomy even with limited context, while a highly experienced delegate might still need a check-in on an unusually high-stakes call.

Common mistake

Choosing a delegation level based on general trust in the person, rather than the specific stakes and context of the task at hand.

items.prompt: L2's example level-setting sentence does three things at once. What are they?
choices: States a deadline, assigns a budget, and names a backup contact
States the level (research and recommend), names a specific check-in trigger (finalists, before signing), and explicitly frees the delegate from needing approval on the parts that don't matter
Apologizes for the ambiguity, restates the task, and thanks the delegate
Lists every possible vendor option to consider
items.explanation: A good level-setting sentence combines all three: the level itself, a specific trigger point for check-in, and explicit freedom on everything else — this is what turns a vague delegation into an actionable one.
items.reference:
"Go ahead and research options — loop me in once you've got it narrowed to two or three finalists, before you sign anything. I don't need to be involved in the research itself."

Why: this single sentence states the level, the check-in trigger, and the delegate's freedom, all at once.
items.learnMore:
Three jobs, one sentence

A level-setting sentence is doing real, compact work — it's worth noticing all three components rather than treating it as just a polite way of assigning a task.

Common mistake

Naming a check-in point without also explicitly freeing the delegate on everything else, which can accidentally read as broader oversight than intended.

items.prompt: Why does the example sentence explicitly say "I don't need to be involved in the research itself"?

It's meant to discourage the delegate from asking questions at all
It has no effect on how the delegation is interpreted
items.explanation: Naming a check-in trigger alone could be read as 'check in about everything, but especially this' — explicitly stating what does NOT need approval prevents that misreading and keeps the delegate's autonomy clear on the rest.

items.prompt: If a report nails a Level 3 delegation (a strong, well-reasoned recommendation), what does that suggest for next time?
choices: Nothing — the level should always stay the same regardless of past performance
They may have earned a higher level (like Level 4-5) for similar future tasks — the level reflects demonstrated context for that kind of decision, not a fixed rating of the person
They should be given full autonomy on every future task, in every domain, immediately
The manager should never delegate that type of task to them again
items.explanation: Demonstrated success at one level is real evidence for shifting up the level on similar future tasks — but it's specific to that kind of decision, not a blanket promotion to full autonomy everywhere.
items.reference:
Level is a living assessment of demonstrated context for THIS KIND of decision — not a fixed rating of the person overall.

Why: the same person can reasonably sit at different levels for different tasks.
items.learnMore:
Levels are per-task-type, not per-person

Someone can reasonably be at Level 5 on a task they've done many times and Level 2 on something genuinely new to them — thinking of delegation level as a single trait of the person, rather than a per-task assessment, misses this.

Common mistake

Treating a delegate's overall seniority as automatically determining their level on every specific task, regardless of their context for that particular decision.

items.prompt: Does earning a higher delegation level on vendor evaluations automatically mean the same person should get full autonomy on, say, hiring decisions?
choices: Yes — trust earned in one domain transfers completely to every other domain
No — the level is specific to demonstrated context for THAT KIND of decision; a different domain (like hiring) would need its own level assessment
Yes, but only after exactly one year at the company
No — earned trust in one domain should never transfer to any other domain at all
items.explanation: Context and demonstrated judgment are domain-specific — strong performance on vendor evaluations is real evidence for that domain, but doesn't automatically establish context for an unrelated domain like hiring.
items.reference:
Level is a living assessment of demonstrated context for THIS KIND of decision — not a fixed rating of the person overall.

Why: the same person can reasonably sit at different levels for different tasks.
items.learnMore:
Levels are per-task-type, not per-person

Someone can reasonably be at Level 5 on a task they've done many times and Level 2 on something genuinely new to them — thinking of delegation level as a single trait of the person, rather than a per-task assessment, misses this.

Common mistake

Treating a delegate's overall seniority as automatically determining their level on every specific task, regardless of their context for that particular decision.
